articles.text: The first Tuesday in May is National Teacher Appreciation Day, and it marks the start of Teacher Appreciation Week. To honor the little-known holiday the Post checked in with some Piedmont teachers to open a window into the classroom, so to speak. Among the district’s many outstanding teachers, Ted Sherman (6th grade), Marna Chamberlain (Honors Physics), and Aaron Barlin (English, ASB Advisor) have met the crises head on to embody the high school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable.” Two years ago the high school started the year without a Physics teacher. Last year, 2019-2020, Marna Chamberlain volunteered to teach the course for the first time, though she wasn’t sure how or where she would find the extra time that would be required. When schools closed in March 2020 she found herself teaching new material in a format completely foreign to nearly everyone – distance learning. “Between gallery walks, posters and whiteboards, that’s how I would usually run my classroom for feedback. It is called formative assessment, which are not graded but I get to see where students are,” Chamberlain explained. In the first months of the pandemic teachers were not even allowed to make kits to send home to do projects at home. Chamberlain ended up videotaping labs performed in her kitchen and constantly tried to keep the material fresh by using different mediums and applications. “You think about what works best, and you change it – and you keep changing it. If you do the same thing every day kids will say, ughh,” she said. 60 hours a week, every single week.” she said. As a hands-on teacher, the switch to screenbased learning was not easy, and eventually she experienced a case of vertigo from the stress of staring at a monitor for hours and hours. Students have taken notice of their teachers’ efforts throughout the school district. articles.text: New CDC mask guide officially adopted by California Even though the number of new COVID-19 cases is trending downward in Alameda County, it is not yet meeting the benchmarks to move into the least restrictive tier for reopening its economy as of yesterday, Tuesday, May 4. The state did move San Francisco County into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier, this week. The looser restrictions will become effective this Friday, May 7. San Francisco is the only county in the Bay Area that has been moved into the yellow tier. Most other counties, including Alameda County, are in the orange, or moderate, tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Solano County is the only Bay Area county in the more restrictive red tier, or substantial tier. Alameda County moved out of the red tier on March 30. The positivity rate for Alameda County is 1.2 percent as of yesterday, a slight decrease from last week. The positivity rate has not been above 2 percent since February 25. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 87,326 – an increase of 1,643 new cases week-over-week. There have been 27,179 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,555 cases in Hayward. Another 47 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,538. The county has met orange tier metrics for several weeks but has not yet met benchmarks to move into the yellow tier. To move up into the yellow tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 2 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 3.7 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 2 percent in Alameda County. In the yellow tier, most indoor operations are allowed with modifications. Indoor gyms, bars, museums, and family entertainment centers can all increase capacity. The entire color tier system is scheduled to be discontinued next month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. A mask mandate for indoor activities and crowded outdoor spaces will likely remain in place until further notice. Five new cases of COVID- 19 have been reported in Piedmont across the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. articles.text: Over 95 percent of adult Piedmonters – some 7,900 people – have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, May 2, according to Alameda County Public Health Department. In addition, more than 66 percent of Piedmonters are now fully vaccinated, representing over 5,500 people. The sky-high rates of vaccination amongst City residents begs the question – will Piedmont soon be fully vaccinated? While 100 percent vaccination might not be reached, it remains a distinct possibility. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – well below national averages, according to polls released last month by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. This mirrors goals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reach “herd immunity” nationwide – a situation where enough people are immune to COVID-19 to control its spread. Piedmont is quickly closing in on that goal. The City’s high vaccination rate is likely due to several factors. Data from across the country has shown that wealthier areas have the highest vaccination rates, and Piedmont is one of the wealthiest communities in California. The Census estimates that about 21 percent of the City’s population is age 65 years or older, a group receiving priority for vaccine. Piedmont also has many people considered essential front-line workers, such as doctors and nurses. Vaccination rates are rising countywide, and appointments seem to be more available than in recent weeks. Over 1.45 million doses have been administered in Alameda County as of press time, and more than 45 percent of the whole county has been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 44 percent of the population has been fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the county. Options from Pfizer and Moderna require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use in the county after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. Alameda County began using the Johnson & Johnson vaccine last week after the CDC recommended its use be paused for 10 days. A small number of blood clotting cases connected to the vaccine were investigated, and it was found that the benefits of a third vaccine supplier outweighed the exceedingly small risk of blood clots. The CDC has confirmed 17 cases of a blood clotting disorder out of some 8 million people who have received the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. There have been three reported deaths due to the blood clots. Most of the blood clot cases were in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms typically occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clot disorder appears to be extremely rare, people who receive the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents ages 16 and older. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16, and the pharmaceutical company will likely soon get authorization for their vaccine for children ages 12 to 15. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines As of May 4, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. The state has administered about 30.7 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 13 million Californians, about 41 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. pages.text: Wednesday, May 5, 2021 3 Covid News Could Piedmont reach 100 percent vaccination? Hesitancy to COVID-19 vaccines is low in Alameda County By Barry Eitel Over 95 percent of adult Piedmonters – some 7,900 people – have received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of Sunday, May 2, according to Alameda County Public Health Department. In addition, more than 66 percent of Piedmonters are now fully vaccinated, representing over 5,500 people. The sky-high rates of vaccination amongst City residents begs the question – will Piedmont soon be fully vaccinated? While 100 percent vaccination might not be reached, it remains a distinct possibility. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – well below national averages, according to polls released last month by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. This mirrors goals from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to reach “herd immunity” nationwide – a situation where enough people are immune to COVID-19 to control its spread. Piedmont is quickly closing in on that goal. The City’s high vaccination rate is likely due to several factors. Data from across the country has shown that wealthier areas have the highest vaccination rates, and Piedmont is one of the wealthiest communities in California. The Census estimates that about 21 percent of the City’s population is age 65 years or older, a group receiving priority for vaccine. Piedmont also has many people considered essential front-line workers, such as doctors and nurses. Vaccination rates are rising countywide, and appointments seem to be more available than in recent weeks. Over 1.45 million doses have been administered in Alameda County as of press time, and more than 45 percent of the whole county has been fully vaccinated. In Oakland, 44 percent of the population has been fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the county. Options from Pfizer and Moderna require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use in the county after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. Alameda County began using the Johnson & Johnson vaccine last week after the CDC recommended its use be paused for 10 days. A small number of blood clotting cases connected to the vaccine were investigated, and it was found that the benefits of a third vaccine supplier outweighed the exceedingly small risk of blood clots. The CDC has confirmed 17 cases of a blood clotting disorder out of some 8 million people who have received the Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine. There have been three reported deaths due to the blood clots. Most of the blood clot cases were in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms typically occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Even though the blood clot disorder appears to be extremely rare, people who receive the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents ages 16 and older. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16, and the pharmaceutical company will likely soon get authorization for their vaccine for children ages 12 to 15. Alameda County has a form to receive notifications about available appointments at covid-19. acgov.org/vaccines As of May 4, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. The state has administered about 30.7 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 13 million Californians, about 41 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. HISTORY OF COVID IN PIEDMONT Date Total Cases New % Increase Fatality SF moves into yellow tier; Alameda County doesn’t meet benchmarks yet New CDC mask guide officially adopted by California By Barry Eitel Even though the number of new COVID-19 cases is trending downward in Alameda County, it is not yet meeting the benchmarks to move into the least restrictive tier for reopening its economy as of yesterday, Tuesday, May 4. The state did move San Francisco County into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier, this week. The looser restrictions will become effective this Friday, May 7. San Francisco is the only county in the Bay Area that has been moved into the yellow tier. Most other counties, including Alameda County, are in the orange, or moderate, tier, the second-least restrictive tier. Solano County is the only Bay Area county in the more restrictive red tier, or substantial tier. Alameda County moved out of the red tier on March 30. The positivity rate for Alameda County is 1.2 percent as of yesterday, a slight decrease from last week. The positivity rate has not been above 2 percent since February 25. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 87,326 – an increase of 1,643 new cases week-over-week. There have been 27,179 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,555 cases in Hayward. Another 47 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,538. The county has met orange tier metrics for several weeks but has not yet met benchmarks to move into the yellow tier. To move up into the yellow tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 2 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 3.7 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 2 percent in Alameda County. In the yellow tier, most indoor operations are allowed with modifications. Indoor gyms, bars, museums, and family entertainment centers can all increase capacity. The entire color tier system is scheduled to be discontinued next month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. A mask mandate for indoor activities and crowded outdoor spaces will likely remain in place until further notice. Five new cases of COVID- 19 have been reported in Piedmont across the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 181. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters is hosting a public discussion with Alameda County District Attorney Nancy O’Malley tomorrow, Thursday, May 6 starting at 4 p.m. The event is free and open to all community members. To register for the Zoom event, visit https:// www.lwvpiedmont.org/content. a spx?page_id= 40 02&club_ id=601389&item_id=1256825. It will be recorded and posted on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont website for those who cannot join live. O’Malley will describe the work by her department with abused and homeless women, helping them move beyond trauma into a positive future. She will also address the many challenges COVID-19 has posed, and the ways in which the current lack of civility in politics is impeding the pace and scale of progress for women who suffer from violence. Passage of the Violence Against Women Act was held up due to politics, and funding for the Victims Crime Act, which provides resources to states for victims of crime, was also reduced. O’Malley is a nationally recognized expert on issues involving violence against women, violence against persons with disabilities, and interpersonal violence including sexual assault, domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, stalking, and human exploitation and trafficking. She serves in the office that dates to a time when Earl Warren was the Alameda County D.A. before becoming United States Supreme Court Chief Justice. O’Malley is the first woman to serve as the County’s District Attorney.

articles.text: City Council approves proposal from consulting firm At a May 3 meeting, Piedmont’s City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting to prepare updates to the city’s Housing Element. The state has announced it will require the construction of 587 new housing units in Piedmont by the end of the next Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) cycle in 2031. The City’s current Housing Element of the General Plan was adopted in 2011 and outlines the city’s housing goals from 2015 to 2023. The city is close to meeting, and surpassing, the amount of housing units mandated by the RHNA 2015-2023 cycle, according to a 2020 annual progress report. Piedmont has issued building permits for the construction of 73 new units out of a mandated 60 units by the end of next year, 2022. The State of California requires that each jurisdiction’s housing element be updated every eight years and certified by the State. While most portions of a General Plan are updated every 20 to 25 years, State law requires that the Housing Element be updated every eight years. Housing Element planning periods are referred to as “cycles.” The 6th RHNA cycle will require 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current cycle, representing a 979% increase. The expected allocation includes 163 very low-income units, 94 low-income units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate-income units. On March 2, the city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. Lisa Wise Consulting, Inc. (LWC) submitted the only proposal received. The cost of the next Housing Element policy document that the firm will prepare is estimated at $691,000, with $172,000 earmarked for public engagement and outreach. “With approval of LWC as the lead housing consultant, the City moves forward with planning to meet the mandates set by the State of California, starting with meetings of the new Piedmont Housing Advisory Committee on May19 and June 15,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson wrote. “We are confident that the Piedmont community will come together to share ideas and expertise to solve the region’s housing crisis.” Housing Advisory Committee meetings this month and next will highlight results of the citywide fair housing survey and “pinnable” map tools, both of which closed for public comment in April and were funded through a $160,000 grant awarded to Piedmont by California Senate Bill (SB) 2 planning grant program, explained Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. LWC is expected to present their analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. Interested residents are invited to participate in these meetings. articles.text: The Oakland Center of the Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) study, directed by Piedmont resident, Dr. Steve Sidney, currently has job postings for a 35-year follow-up exam of study participants who were first examined in 1985-1986. The CARDIA study, funded by the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute, is a longitudinal study of black and white men and women who were 18-30 years old at the beginning of the study and who have been followed for the development of heart disease risk factors and disease. More than 900 published scientific articles have resulted from the CARDIA study thus far. This will be the 10th examination for study participants who were initially recruited from four centers around the country, including Kaiser Permanente (KP) Health Plan members from the Berkeley-Oakland area. The examination will be conducted by the KP Northern California Division of Research at its research clinic located in the Mosswood Building, 3505 Broadway in Oakland. Positions are available for scheduling examinations, conducting exam interviews and study procedures, data management, and managing the mailing of equipment and supplies for aspects of the study conducted at the homes of participants. These positions will start in May or June of this year and end during the summer of 2022. Training will be provided. If you would like more information, please contact Dr. Sidney at steve.sidney@kp.org. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Dr. Gutlaizer and Ellen and Liza Konnert

articles.text: As I was scrolling through my news feed several weeks ago, ironically enough, I came across an article about a “No-Tech” contest. Yes, it’s true. Reviews.com was looking for a lucky “I can’t live without tech” individual to go without technology for 24 hours. That the contest was for 24 hours only was in itself startling to me. They went on to clarify that applicants need not apply unless the thought of no technology for 24 hours induced a panic attack. To support the contestant, a lock box safe to store each of the tech culprits and a $200 gift card to build a survival kit would be provided. The contest prompted me to think about our use of, and dependency on, technology over the past year and its influence on every aspect of occupation. The American Occupational Therapy Association identifies 8 areas of occupation: • Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) • Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADLs) • Education • Work • Play • Leisure • Social Participation • Rest and Sleep Technology has been interwoven in all 8 occupations of life in one way or another as a result of the global pandemic. Don’t get me wrong, I am thankful for technology. It helped all of us make it through the past 15 months. However, as counties shift to less restrictive tiers and we begin to return to a way of life that is less dependent on technology, can we Are your kids spending too much time on tech devices? – especially our students – wean away from screens and willingly engage in daily life activities that do not involve technology? I decided to find out. As part of a handwriting exercise for my students (yes, a paper and pencil task), I asked them to respond to the writing prompt, “If I went without tech for 24 hours, I would want/need the following in my No Tech survival kit.” To my pleasant surprise (and frankly, relief), the question was not met with gasps or “I don’t know.” Students listed all that is music to an occupational therapist’s ears. Their lists were rich in areas of play, leisure and socialization. Examples of items in their kits and activities included: family, friends, pets, reading books, board and card games, baking supplies, crafts and hobbies, hiking, camping, fishing, golf, and basketball. We have not lost them. So as the school year is quickly coming to an end, now is the time to make plans about the role of technology for the summer and set expectations about screen use. As a family, build your own “No Tech” survival kit. How about a “No Tech Tuesday” for each Tuesday of the summer? A weekend No Tech survival kit? Demonstrate that you too can engage in “occupations of life” without technology. On a final note, there happened to be one student whose initial response to my assignment of no technology was “this would be impossible for me.” He went on to consider the challenge and came up with the reply, “I would just rest.” How amazingly insightful. So don’t delay. Make your summertime survival kit and enjoy occupations of play, leisure, social participation and of course rest and sleep. Have a wonderful less-tech summer! Kimberly Bonacum is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional questions, she can be contacted at mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 6 love a good service project. Recently they had the opportunity to help out at Oakland’s Elizabeth House (www.oakehouse. org), which offers a residence to women with children who have experienced the poverty of homelessness, violence, and addiction. The facility supports women and children in their transition to independence by empowering them with the tools to rebuild their lives. The House’s yards needed some TLC, and Troop 6 was up for the challenge. The first phase of the project was weeding and removing unusable garden beds as well as repairing bikes. A total of 20 Scouts, seven adults, and several of the children of the house pitched in to make fast work of the project. Three green bins and over 20 garden bags later, the space was transformed. The next phase of the project will involve building and planting new garden beds, and if funds can be raised, installing a stone patio which will enable the residents to more fully enjoy their outdoor space. To learn more about Elizabeth House and volunteer for future projects, contact Lisa Gros of Troop 6 at: (lgros@rocketmail.com). Members of Piedmont Scouts Troop 6 from Corpus Christi Church gathered to help the staff at Elizabeth House in Oakland cleaning up the garden, replacing some planting beds, and even repairing some bikes.

When the pandemic is finally over, they will probably stick together because they have persevered together. Everyone’s always rooting for the high school sweethearts. Type three: The germaphobe couple. This is the couple who somehow confessed their feelings to each other, but there’s no bubble for them. Even when they get within 50-yards of one another, they wish they had a hazmat suit on because one can never be too careful. This couple also spends most of their time on their phones calling one another because going outside is just too risky. This couple will go on a hike as a date, but the twist is this hike will be nowhere near civilization. Another date night idea would be to go to a romantic drive-in movie theatre. Type four: The couple that never talks to each other but somehow is still together. This is the couple where both people forgot they were in a relationship until someone reminded them. It’s not that they don’t feel affection towards one another, it’s just they are both antisocial, spend most of their time listening to music, and prefer the company of cats. The spouse is always there, whether you want it or not. And there are no distractions, like eating in restaurants or spending time with other couples. What if you don’t like the way your significant other eats? You have to watch this three times a day, seven days a week. And you can’t even go on vacation. articles.text: Residents participate by presenting Heritage Tree nominations Sue Herrick and Cameron Wolfe Jim Horner The City of Piedmont opted for a virtual Arbor Day celebration this year in light of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is still prohibiting events with large gatherings. A 20-minute video, created by KCOM, the city’s TV station, and produced by Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap, celebrates the city’s diverse urban forest by highlighting all 19 Heritage Trees throughout Piedmont. The tree, or group of trees, should exhibit three qualities. The tree should be an integral part of an architectural theme, or play an important role in framing or screening a building or other civic feature. It should be recognized as part of a memorial or is an outstanding remnant of early civic plantings, and it should represent an outstanding example of the species, in its age, size and form, is unique to the City, or is an outstanding example of California flora. The Arbor Day celebration spans four years of nominations, from 2018, when the Heritage Tree policy began, through this year. In the video, community members introduce the trees they have nominated. When the original nominator was unavailable, a stand-in resident introduced the tree, explained Patty Dunlap. Piedmont resident Zack Parisa served as the guest speaker. The video also included submissions from a chalk drawing contest in which the city’s young artists depicted their favorite city trees using colored chalks. The video was shot and edited by KCOM’s Jason Liao. “[The video] turned out beautifully and is a great educational piece. The Park Commission is really excited to present it,” Dunlap said. Formal portraits of this year’s five designated Heritage Trees will be taken by Park Commissioner Brian Mahany and should be available next week. With the final portraits, the city will be able to populate an interactive map of all Heritage Trees. “With the interactive map, people will be able to click coordinates and get exact locations where the Heritage Tree or cluster of trees is located,” Dunlap said. It is a long-standing tradition to plant a tree on Arbor Day. This year, the city will be planting a tree honoring the life of Ralston Louie, a Piedmont graduate who passed away unexpectedly this year. The commemorative tree, a Yulan Magnolia, will be planted in Dracena Park. The video can be viewed on Youtube or on the City’s website by visiting https://piedmont. ca.gov/government/city_news___ notifications/arbor_day_2021. You can also visit www.piedmont. ca.gov to learn more about the heritage trees; featured trees are listed below. Coast Redwood, nominated by Cameron Wolfe and Susan Herrick Residents Cameron Wolfe and Susan Herrick, independently of each other, nominated the first Heritage Tree for the city of Piedmont. It is the large Coast Redwood in Piedmont Park; the tree first served as a community “holiday greeting tree” in the early 1970s, Wolfe explained. “[It] is appropriate [as a Heritage tree] because it is a Sequoia Sempervirens, probably the most significant tree in California, better known as the coastal, or California Redwood,” said Wolfe. “This tree really has a remarkable history. Many, many generations of children, and now adults, have come here to celebrate the holiday season and light the lights on this beautiful tree, and Cameron and I both felt it had such a significance in the history of our beautiful city,” Herrick said. Highland Poplars, nominated by Jim Horner Park Commissioner Jim Horner nominated a cluster of Highland Poplar trees forming the backdrop of the Exedra at Highland and Magnolia. “They are really an important aesthetic contribution to the city. And I think it’s amusing - that there are Highland Poplars right on Highland Avenue,” he said. “They provide a wonderful winter scrim of lacework branches, and in the summertime, billowing green leaves.” Grove of Dawn Redwoods, nominated by Lyle Gordon Resident Lyle Gordon nominated a grove of Dawn Redwoods in 2018. “I thought they were really interesting as one of the three types of conifers that lose their needles in the fall, and then get them back in the Spring,” he said. Southern Magnolia, nominated by Betsy Goodman Park Commissioner Betsy Goodman nominated a Southern Magnolia four years ago when the Heritage Tree program began. “I asked [former Public Works Supervisor] Dave Frankel, what is the most beautiful tree in PiedBetsey Goodman mont? We both agreed that it was this particular Southern Magnolia - it’s magnificent with arching camber, and is evergreen with beautiful white blossoms,” Goodman said. “It is definitely worthy of being a Heritage Tree.” Eastern Redbud, nominated by Lisa Kieraldo Lisa Kieraldo nominated a cluster of Eastern Redbuds at the Wildwood Avenue entrance to Piedmont Park in 2019. Horner provided background on the tree’s significance and confirmed they had been nominated twice by Kieraldo. “They are a wonderful entry point marker for the park and high school,” Horner said. Redwood, nominated by Cindy Rafton Another large Redwood has Heritage Tree status - nominated by Cindy Rafton in 2019. This tree, located on Requa Road, marked the entrance to the early 20th century Ransom Bridge Girls’ School, which opened in 1919. “I love this big tree, I look at it every day from my kitchen window,” Rafton said with a smile. Coast Live Oak, nominated by the Brumfiel boys A Coast Live Oak in Piedmont Park was nominated by Will, Finn and Max Brumfiel in 2019. Arbor Day guest speaker Zack Parisa “We call it ‘the climbing tree,” said 8-year-old Will. “We love to climb the tree with our friends.” Evergreen Dogwoods, nominated by Bobbe Stehr and Mark Enea The four Himalayan Dogwoods that line the entrance to City Hall were nominated by residents Bobbe Stehr and Public Works staffer Mark Enea in 2019. “They are spectacular, because they are evergreen, stately, and in the spring, they produce these fabulous, large, cream-colored flowers that cover the entire tree,” Stehr said. “They are real showstoppers.” Eileen Ruby in 2020. “I walk by this tree all the time, and it’s beautiful in every season. It’s beautiful in Spring, when it’s budding, and the summers, when it’s in full, green foliage, and in the fall when the leaves turn red,” she said. “It’s situated perfectly at the entrance to the Japanese tree house.” Cherry Walk, nominated by Nancy McHugh The Akebono Cherry Tree walk in Piedmont Park was nominated by Nancy McHugh in 2020. Valerie Matzger introduced McHugh’s nomination. “Many of them have been planted in memory of someone Grove of Coast Redwoods, who lived in Piedmont, or a loved nominated by Gail Lombardi person who passed away. You’ll and the Hoe and Hope Garden see tags on these trees, acknowlClub edging who they are honoring,” A grove of 18 Coast Redwoods Matzger said. in the planted triangle at Wildwood and Magnolia Avenues was nominated by Gail Lombardi in 2019. “It’s a quiet, forest-like respite between two busy streets, going to and from Grand Avenue. Pedestrians, dog-walkers, and residents can come here and experience a sense of quiet and calm,” she said. Japanese Maple, nominated by Eileen Ruby A Japanese Maple located in Piedmont Park was nominated by Coast Live Oak, nominated by Tami and Mark Becker Tami and Mark Becker nominated a Coast Live Oak in Dracena Park in 2020. “It’s phenomenal, and it’s a California native. We just really enjoy its presence here in Dracena Park,” said Tami. “We’ve lived across the street [from the tree] for 27 years. It’s been an anchor to this park and the Dracena lawn,” added Mark. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team is 3-0 after winning two more games, both on the road. They beat St. Joseph 70-43 on Thursday, April 29, and overpowered Hayward 69-28 the next day. “The game with St. Joe went back and forth. But in the second half, we were hustling and diving on the floor. That stuff is contagious,” said coach Bryan Gardere with a grin. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team opened their season with a 1-0 shutout of Alameda at Thompson Field on Thursday, April 29. Zach Luna scored the lone goal in the 30th minute in quick pressing fashion, while Alameda had few scoring chances. “On a horrible field, we were playing in a particular way that will differ from when we get back to Witter,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan of Alameda’s patchy surface. “With the players we have, I’m expecting to play more possession-based soccer.” The two schools had a solid rivalry in 2019-2020. The Highlanders beat Alameda 3-0 early in the season but lost 4-0 in the final week of the 2020 season. Alameda went on to win the league title. “It’s always a good game with Alameda, you have to come ready to play. It’s a good first game to have,” added Sullivan. Thursday’s game featured the Highlanders playing a high defensive line in the first half, resulting in the Hornets often struggling to get the ball past midfield. The press enabled Luna to score the eventual game-winner after taking the ball in front of the net and rolling it past Alameda’s keeper. “I think the boys noticed that they weren’t very strong good in the back. We nicked the ball high up the field and that’s how we got the goal. We put Zach in the middle of the midfield; he’s a bit older and wiser, and he did quite well in that central role. He got right in behind Aiden [Woolwine], won the ball in a great area and got the goal,” he explained. Piedmont had another chance to score earlier after striker Aiden Woolwine won a set piece, leading to Connor Curtis launching a curling pass to the feet of Ian Work, who forced a diving save by the Hornets’ keeper. articles.text: Traveling to San Lorenzo for their first game of the season, Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team produced a 1-0 victory on Thursday, April 29. “We have really good energy on the team right now,’ said veteran coach Dan Chubbock. “Arroyo has improved over the years and they were without a couple of their best players. They are definitely a school we can’t overlook.” The Highlanders will play a return match with Arroyo tonight at Witter Field, then play longtime soccer rival Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, May 6. The two games in two days is a schedule created by the league and frowned upon by coaches. “The league scheduled all the games for us this year, I definitely didn’t like that draw when the WACC released schedules,” confirmed Chubbock. The shutout of Arroyo came with plenty of help from the defense, and sophomore goalkeeper Morgan Hunt was rarely challenged. Piedmont’s goal was scored by Zenobia Pellissier-Lloyd 20 minutes into the game after receiving a pass from Zoe Wolfers. After receiving the ball around midfield, Wolfers played a perfectly driven through-ball to Pellissier-Lloyd as she made a run behind Arroyo’s back line. On her way to the goal, Pellissier-Lloyd shrugged off the Don’s centerback, who fell to the ground as the Piedmont attacker sent a left-footed shot past the charging keeper for the score. “It was a nice through-ball from Zoe into Zenobia, who had a nice finish with her left foot,” said Chubbock. “We only had a few practices before the game, so we’re still really building our chemistry,” SAID described Pellissier-Lloyd. “But we were able to build the ball up from the back, and Zoe played a ball through and I was able to get by the defender,” Piedmont played in a 4-4-2 diamond formation, allowing Chubbock to load the midfield with four central midfielders including Emily Fitzgerald as an attacking midfielder behind the striker, Pellissier-Lloyd. “We’re finding the right role for Emily to utilize her strengths. She’s definitely an attacking player,” said Chubbock of last year’s team leading scorer. The Highlanders will use the same formation against Arroyo tonight, according to Chubbock. Some adjustments will be made in the game with O’Dowd to prevent BOD runners charging down the wing. “We’re going to stick with this system because it allows us to adapt during the game defensively. That obviously will change for some opponents.” With today’s game against Arroyo and Thursday’s Bishop O’Dowd match exactly 24-hours apart, Piedmont is expected to enlist several J.V. players against tonight in order to conserve some energy for Thursday’s match with the Dragons. “We will likely have five JV players for Wednesday’s game. We want to do well with integrating players from J.V. this year, especially with no NCS playoffs.” added Chubbock. articles.text: The Piedmont High Mountain Bike Team is back in action with races at Sigma Six Ranch in Lower Lake on consecutive Sundays, April 25 and May 2. The 6.2-mile course had an estimated 700 feet of elevation gain. The squad brought 15 student-athletes to compete in multiple categories, including Varsity Boys, JV Boys, Sophomore Boys, Sophomore Girls and Freshman Boys. The races were hosted by the National Interscholastic Cycling Association’s NorCal Cycling League, in which PHS riders compete with students from Bishop O’Dowd, Head-Royce, San Ramon Valley, Berkeley, Oakland Tech, El Cerrito, Clayton Valley Charter, and local clubs including Oakland Composite, Hayward Composite, and Castro Valley MBT. Will Shields placed 2nd overall in the varsity races on both dates. Shields describes the differences between this years’ time trial runs, compared to races with mass starts in previous years. “Normally we’d do a mass start with four laps of racing against other people, which requires some tactics in sitting behind people, drafting, and being focused on what other people are doing. This year, it’s all about yourself, trying to keep a fast pace and finish under 40 minutes,” he said. But time trials require careful planning. “In a race with a mass start, you want to conserve energy without letting people pass you, plan your attack and respond to people who are attacking. With a time trial, it’s kind of the opposite. You have to use full power as much as possible,” he said. This year the number of riders is greatly reduced because the 2020 season had only one preseason race before the season was canceled due to Covid. Typically, racers must qualify for the varsity division through JV races. “Qualification for varsity is usually done through the previous year’s race results, but because there were so few races last year, the varsity field this year is even smaller,” explained coach Sally Aldridge. articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek. Ruth Bancroft Garden, located in Walnut Creek, will host an Ikebana workshop on Saturday, May 22. Ikebana is the Japanese art of flower arrangements, a tradition that dates back centuries. The workshop will be led by Sharon Suimei Doi, a regular Bancroft Garden exhibitor. She will offer an Ikebana lesson using succulents. Doi will also demonstrate basic Japanese floral arrangement concepts with branches and plant materials that would be found in a dry climate similar to Walnut Creek. Bancroft Garden is known for its extensive succulent and cactus displays. Students will get to work on their own arrangements with the assistance of an instructor. Class fees include a ceramic container, pin frog and plant materials. Students will need to bring their own garden clippers. All COVID-19 protocols will be in effect. Regardless of vaccination status, students will be asked to wear a face mask and create social distancing. Hand sanitizers will be provided. The class will be held from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. on Saturday, May 22. Registration closes on May 19. To obtain tickets, visit: https://www.ruthbancroftgarden. org/event/ikebana-japanese-floral-art-workshop/.

articles.text: Carlos Aguirre Aurora Theatre explores the intersection between art and activism in a recent panel discussion with Bay Area activists. Aguirre has performed both as a hip-hop actor and artists in the Bay Area for over 19 years. He has performed with well-known groups and artists like The Roots, Eryka Badu, Black Eyed Peas, Mary J. Blige, Jam Master Jay, and George Clinton. Flores is a multidisciplinary artist, whose crafts include dancing, acting, and painting. “Aurora Connects” is Aurora Theatre Company’s bi-weekly live broadcast, an “online salon and virtual happy hour.” A broadcast will go live every other Thursday at 5 p.m. on the theatre company’s YouTube channel. Each episode is hosted by theatre Artistic Director Josh Costello and Associate Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Costello was appointed artistic director in 2019 following a national search. At Aurora, he has directed, among others, Exit Strategy, The Importance of Being Earnest, Detroit, and the award-winning world premiere of Jonathan Spector’s Eureka Day. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. An Oakland-native, she was Artistic Associate and a resident artist at the Oregon Shakespeare Festival for six seasons. To watch the panel discussion, visit https://www.auroratheatre. org/auroraconnects.

articles.text: Louise M. Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco San Francisco Symphony has announced the return of live concerts at Davies Hall beginning tomorrow, May 6. Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen leads the symphony in live performances for medical professionals in concerts on May 6 and May 7, and tickets will go on sale tomorrow for seven additional concerts. The list of guest conductors includes: Jeremy Denk, International Concert Pianist James Gaffigan, Trondheim Symphony Orchestra & Opera (Norway) Ken-David Masur, Milwaukee Symphony Orchestra Joseph Young, Berkeley Symphony Joshua Weilerstein, Chamber Orchestra of Lausanne (Switzerland) “A friend recently told me that we need to just start,” said Salonen. “I feel joy and relief at finally being able to do just that with the San Francisco Symphony. We go into these concerts having worked as a unit to bring music into homes in unique and meaningful ways this year. We now welcome audiences into our home – something we didn’t realize we had taken for granted.” After nearly a year of vacancy, Davies Hall will be packed with performances from tomorrow through June 25. Program highlights for the first two concerts include Jean Sibelius’ Rakastava, George Walker’s Lyric for Strings, Carl Nielsen’s Little Suite for Strings, Caroline Shaw’s Entr’acte, and Edvard Grieg’s From Holberg’s Time Suite. All concerts will be approximately 75 minutes in length and will be performed without intermissions. Instrumentation and orchestra size is planned in accordance with city guidelines and will vary. All San Francisco Symphony performances will require proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test as well as mask-wearing. To comply with current health restrictions, there will be significantly reduced concert hall capacity, contactless tickets, assigned seats, and increased ventilation. You can visit sfsymphony.org/safety. “I want to thank every member of the San Francisco Symphony family – from our Orchestra colleagues and COVID Health and Safety task force, to our incredibly supportive Board leadership – for working creatively together to make these concerts happen so quickly,” said SF Symphony CEO Mark Hanson. “There is nothing that compares to experiencing music together in a physical space. After 14 months without sharing these human connections with each other, we simply cannot wait to resume performing for our community on the stage of Davies Symphony Hall.” To obtain tickets and to view a full list of programming, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/.
articles.title: Tickets available for performances through June 25

For 40 years the pair has performed for audiences around the world with a penchant for re-imagined jazz classics and pop-music billboard charters. Their albums have themselves regularly appeared on top 10 Billboard Contemporary Jazz charts, and their SF Jazz performances are highly anticipated. Living Jazz created the calland-response series in 2020 in response to the current health pandemic and subsequent venue closures. The unique series of intimate conversations features some of the world’s most iconic jazz musicians in an effort to provide exposure to meaningful, in-depth conversation by jazz luminaries. The musicians are considered jazz legends, and will speak candidly about the inspiration behind their music, struggles and victories. Audience members will be invited to ask questions and actively participate in an open question-and-answer session. To reserve your spot for the discussion, visit https://www. sfarts.org/event/living-jazz-presents-call--response-tuck--patti-2TGo2vUeVpjFhgr6wJenP5.

articles.text: In many ways the well-made and superbly acted Eye in the Sky is reassuring. But it also can be chillingly disconcerting. It begins as a straightforward surveillance of a militant group associated with the East Africa terrorist organization Al Shabab. Then unexpectedly it morphs into something far more serious and morally hazardous. What is initially being watched – from 20,000 feet by an unseen, eerily quiet drone – is a house in Nairobi, Kenya, where a meeting is taking place between highly placed Shabab leaders, to include a woman, a British citizen, who has aligned herself with the organization. The original plan is to raid the house and capture those inside. But using a cyborg beetle, an agent (Barkhad Abdi), is sitting outside on the street and using a control no larger than a cell phone. He positions the small beetle with a miniaturized camera inside the house where it reveals that in another room several suicide bombers are preparing to put on explosive vests. articles.text: Piedmont’s long-running Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The film will be followed by a Question & Answer session with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler. The film is free by registering at diversityfilmseries.org, and clicking on the “Register for The Social Dilemma button”. The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good – even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. articles.text: The stop-motion, animated feature Coraline is a tour de force of imagination. Though made to be shown in stereoscopic 3-D, even in 2-D it is vivid and rich with a panoply of colors and strange, interesting characters. But for all of its technical wonder and labor-intensive filming – the characters are three-dimensional figures that are moved ever so slightly, a single frame at a time, it’s hard to enthusiastically recommend this film for children. Caroline is a dark and sinister narrative which takes a young girl’s fantasy and turns it into a gothic nightmare. Of course, all fairytales have a distinctly dark side to them. Dorothy follows the yellow brick road only to meet the Wicked Witch. Alice falls down the rabbit hole. And certainly Harry Potter, for all of his deft ability with magic, encounters evil that takes many forms and threatens his very existence. And so it is with Coraline, who recently moved from Michigan to Ashland, Oregon. She and her parents are living in a Victorian rooming house called The Pink Palace filled with eccentric boarders. Feeling lonely and bored, and finding her parents distracted and cranky as they work intensely on a gardening catalogue, she explores the house and soon discovers a hidden door in her room that opens into a narrow tunnel (a rabbit hole?) and a parallel world. In this mirror universe, however, her new parents are attentive to her every need, and her room is wonderfully inviting. The only disconcerting aspect is that everyone she meets has buttons instead of eyes – something she is willing to overlook. So seductive is this new world, where flowers bloom in the moonlight, where all is a kaleidoscope of colors, she begins to find it harder and harder to return to her real life and her real parents. And, of course, her newly discovered mother encourages her to remain forever. It all seems so perfect. But as a talking cat suggests, perhaps there is more to this parallel world than first meets the eye (or button). And perhaps all of this goodwill and attention is a bit suspicious. What child doesn’t fantasize about a world in which they are the center of attention, a world in which they feel powerful and have more than a modicum of control over their own lives. Or a world suddenly absent parents who draw boundaries and make rules and all seems so arbitrary. The culmination of this fantasy was captured perfectly in the film Home Alone, when Kevin wakes up in his house and discovers everyone is gone. He wished them gone, and suddenly his wish has come true. He quickly sets out to create a life in which he rules. It’s a rush until it isn’t. Like Kevin, Coraline is soon confronted with more than she can handle. What was a thrill becomes deeply frightening. Will she be able to find her way back to her real world and once again be able to embrace her parents? Nothing is certain. What is surprising about Coraline is that none of the characters are particularly attractive. Even Coraline herself is feisty and a bit ill-tempered. That’s not to say that she should be more like Cinderella; but there has to be an emotional bridge built between the young audience and Coraline. Not even a young neighbor, Wybie, who wants to befriend Coraline, is terribly endearing. In return, she accuses him of being a stalker. Young children ever so easily blur the lines between what is real and what is fantasy and might find the last half of Coraline too intense. The strength of this film is that it is so wonderfully imagined. Based on Neil Gaiman’s book of the same name, which has sold over a million copies worldwide, there clearly is something about the story that resonates with kids. No doubt, all kids love to be scared – a little. Call it the jeepers creepers effect. On the larger-than-life screen, however, its impact may be more than some youngsters can handle. Coraline. Stop-motion animation. Starring the voices of Dakota Fanning, Teri Hatcher, Directed by Henry Selick. Rated PG.

articles.text: If you are like me, the differences between all those buildings with prominent columns on them has always been a little unclear. Maybe today we can begin to sort it out. First, we go back to the Greeks. Their architecture was simpler, characterized by closely spaced columns because their era did not have the spanning capability of the arch. Along came the Romans, who in addition to borrowing heavily from the Greeks, were beneficiaries of the invention of concrete which allowed vaults, domes and arches, leading to a different, more developed architecture. Although the Greek and Roman civilizations were about 1000 years apart at their peaks, in our era the architecture they produced has been conventionally lumped together as Classical Architecture. This Classical Architecture was, and indeed is, pretty amazing. Well thought out with mathematically calculated proportions that are pleasing to the eye and mind, they seem to form a natural part of the universal order. Certainly they have endured over the centuries, having been “revived” numerous times. As this country was being formed in the late 1700’s, most of the new construction was On the spectrum of revival styles, these impressive Piedmont homes tend towards Classical Revival (or Neoclassical). That is because they utilize the classical characteristics of large porticos (covered, columned entries), tall columns and classical orders (note the Ionic and Corinthian columns). They also tend towards formality because of their symmetry – the entry in the center of the building mass with the same balanced facades on each side. strongly influenced by settlers from Europe, especially from England, to which we were attached as colonies. At that time there was a Classical Revival in vogue in Europe. It appeared on this side of the pond as well, and was the start of our Colonial Architecture style. Fast forward 100 years of style preference upswings and downswings to the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 in Chicago – America’s first World’s Fair. With 10 million visitors viewing the pervasive Classical style architecture of the fair developed principally by the architect Daniel Burnham, America was exposed and reawakened to the architecture of antiquity and its colonial past, which we knew principally through our Colonial Architecture. Colonial Revival was born, and was immensely popular, flourishing for decades throughout the country, including California. So, Classical and Colonial Revival styles are stylistically linked, although there are many variants out there. Generally, the “purer” Classical Revival (or Neoclassical) style is more formal and monumental, occurring in larger institutional and civic buildings such as city and state capitals. articles.text: Many may be unfamiliar with kumquats, a petite jewel of the citrus family, where the entire fruit is consumed in one delicious bite, sweet and tart. About the size of a grape, the entire kumquat is eaten, including the skin, which is actually the sweeter part of the fruit. A visit with my mom, who lives in Roseville, included picking a sizeable harvest of kumquats from her backyard tree. Since I had too many to eat at their peak of freshness, I knew I was going to be in for at least a couple of baking projects. Advance tip: Dates, and many dried fruits, will stick together when chopped. To help with an even distribution throughout the tea cake, I spread out the chopped pieces on a plate. When ready to add to the batter, I sprinkle them in and gently fold into the batter so they stay separated. Kumquat Tea Cake Adapted from Nicole Coudal’s My Delicious Blog INGREDIENTS • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, softened • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 1/2 cup sour cream, room temperature • 1/2 cup kumquat puree • 4 tablespoons freshly squeezed orange juice • 2 extra-large eggs • 1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cup all-purpose flour • 3/4 teaspoon baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon baking soda • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt • 1 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped • 1/2 cup dates, coarsely chopped INSTRUCTIONS To puree the kumquats, slice in half crosswise and remove any seeds. Then blitz in a mini-food processor or small blender until nearly smooth. I prefer having a few bits of identifiable rind. Position an oven rack at the lower third position. Preheat oven to 350˚ F. Line an 8.5 x 4.5-inch loaf pan with parchment paper crosswise, then generously butter the exposed ends. Set aside. Combine the flour, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a medium bowl and whisk to combine well. Set aside. In a large mixing bowl, use an electric mixer to cream the softened butter until light and fluffy. Gradually add the sugar and continue beating until sugar is dissolved. Add the eggs, beating to incorporate well, then add the kumquat puree, orange juice and vanilla extract. The mixture will look curdled, but that’s OK. Add one-third of the flour mixture on low speed, then alternate one-half of the sour cream, another one-third of the flour mixture, the remaining sour cream, and end with the flour mixture. Take care to not overmix, using a spatula to complete the incorporation of the flour mixture into the batter. Add the chopped walnuts and dates. Take care to separate the dates, as they are sticky and will tend to clump together. You will want an even distribution of dates and walnuts throughout the batter. Pour the batter into the prepared loaf pan and bake for about 1 hour, until a toothpick inserted in the middle of the loaf comes out clean. Cool in the pan for about 10 minutes, then remove from the pan and transfer to a wire rack to complete cooling. Pictured are: Albert Chen (left), Jim Kao, Pat McSwain, Sue Shepardson, Dick Carter, Melba Yee, Sherry Jacobs, Kathy Gustafson, and Bob Gustafson. Not shown: Andree and Mark Greenberg. On a beautiful, spring Piedmont day on April 28, the Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered for their third week of walks since Covid restrictions were lifted. Thirteen walkers were on hand, including Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Nancy Henn, Sherry Jacobs, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Dick Carter, and firsttime walkers Sue Shepardson and Pat McSwain. The day before their walk the CDC had issued new guidelines for small groups to walk outdoors without masks, but the group agreed that they would continue to wear masks. The previous week the group walked to Dracena Park, a former rock quarry, so they decided to continue their exploration of quarry sites that have become recreation parks. The decision was to visit Davie Tennis Stadium on the Piedmont/Oakland border. The site was the former Piedmont Paving Company quarry and was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by John L Davie, a former mayor and lawyer. The stadium includes five courts and a clubhouse mainly within the Piedmont city limits. After meeting at the Exedra, the group walked behind the Community Hall up to Guilford Avenue and then down a short path to Hazel Lane. They viewed the historic, huge redwood tree in the road just before Requa Road. This tree marked the entrance to Piedmont’s first school, the Ransom-Bridges School, which opened in 1913 on land that is now the Hazel Lane loop. The group went down Requa Road, past the home of Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi, who has provided so much Piedmont history that the walkers have enjoyed. They also noted an impressive gazebo in a backyard perched high above the street on large steel beams. After crossing Wildwood Avenue they went down Prospect Avenue to Oakmont Avenue and then into the tennis stadium. Looking up at the steep rock walls, they saw the slope that was created by the quarry digging decades ago. Players were on the courts, but the historic clubhouse with its collection of vintage racquets and pictures of local tennis greats was closed because of the pandemic. The morning was going by quickly and it was time to head back. The group walked up to Park Lane, over to Lakeshore Avenue and up Harvard Road and back to Prospect. The walkers made their way back to the Exedra by going through Piedmont. They were pleased with its shade provided by the park and pleased to see that water was still flowing in Bushy Dell Creek. The walkers emerged from the park after a leisurely, enjoyable two-mile walk in 90 minutes. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues). Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required by contacting John Wilk at jwilk@piedmont. ca.gov. pages.text: Wednesday, May 5, 2021 25 Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets Do vets ever make house calls? By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Do you know of any vets that will come to the house to help us with our end-of-life goodbyes? Tilly is now 17 and things seem to be going downhill fast. I do not want to take her to our vet to say goodbye. Or entire family would like to be present when we say so long. than one. I’m at a loss, in more ways – Betsy and Tilly the mix Dear Betsy and Tilly: There are many things to consider when saying goodbye to a beloved pet. As hard as it is, working out the details ahead of time is very smart. The fact that you know that your entire family wants to be together to say your farewells is a big step. Some owners find it easier to say goodbye when your pet is having a good day, although others, (like me) find it easier when things are very clearly near the end. In truth, there is no perfect time for euthanasia. I had a friend who used the Rainbow Bridge Vet Services, (founded by Dr. Anthony Smith in 2000) and was very grateful she did. Dr. Smith received his Bachelor’s degree from Stanford and his Doctorate in Veterinary Medicine from UC Davis. He has practiced in a variety of areas in veterinary medicine but eventually re-thought the entire process of euthanasia. For the last two decades, he has been able to help thousands of people navigate the tricky roads of hospice and euthanasia in the privacy of their own homes where they are able to plan ceremonies and grieve as they say goodbye. Email: rainbowbridgevet@ gmail.com or call (or text): 510- 381-3389. Business Hours are Mon-Fri, 8 am-6pm and Saturday 9am-3pm. Sundays are closed. Appointments must be made. Remember, Tilly was lucky to have you and you were lucky to have Tilly for 17 short years. In dog years that’s 119 – truly a wonderful life. –Abby Dear Abby: We were up at Sibley Park eating a picnic lunch and a sizable dog smelled the food and made a beeline for us. I moved our lunch in the nick of time and fortunately the dog was friendly and listened to his owner to leave us alone and continue onward. But it seems everyone has been sharing stories with me that don’t end quite as happily. Are dogs allowed off-leash up there? –Serena, a hiker, dog lover (but no dogs yet) Dear Serena: Dogs are permitted to be off leash in Sibley and other East Bay Regional Parks, although each park has specific rules which are posted at the entrances. The East Bay Regional Park District has heard your concerns and is running a “Be a Pup Pro” campaign right now. It’s never easy to react when a big dog comes over sniffing for food. Essentially the District’s campaign has three basic themes: 1. Bag it and Bin it. Don’t leave your dog deposits on the side of a path for other dog walkers to pick up on their way out. Just slip it in a bag and carry it until you see a trash can. 2. Leash your dog in designated areas like the parking lot, trailheads, picnic areas, paved trails or by the public bathrooms. Again, each park posts specific signs on where a dog needs to be leashed which will prevent unnecessary accidents. 3. Actively keep your dog safe. Don’t permit your dog to mingle with cattle or horses that might be grazing on the grasslands. Definitely watch out for rattlesnakes and even wild rabbits which can bite a dog and infect them. And though it might be a bit inconvenient, carry water. As the weather heats up, our furry friends can dehydrate quickly. You can find an array of inexpensive, lightweight, compact bowls at local pet food shops or online that can squeeze into a pocket and water can be carried in a small container. Remember pavement and rocks can get very hot in the sun which can be hard on even the toughest paws. Right now, brilliant silver-blue lupine, bunches of hot yellow mustard, Scotch broom golds and the gorgeous orange of the California poppies are covering the hillsides, not to mention the shades of green. Recently we even stumbled on a glade of wild cherry blossoms. This year seems to be particularly gorgeous and since you can’t get on a plane to hike in Switzerland right now. Just drive 10 minutes to Skyline and pretend. It’s pawsome. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com. articles.text: On the weekend of April 10-11 Piedmont Scouts from Troop 15 had their first overnight campout since the start of COVID more than one year ago. They went to Camp Tamarancho, a BSA campsite in Marin County. To comply with Marin COVID restrictions, the troop split up into patrols and stayed in their patrols throughout the weekend. All of the Scouts were excited to get back to nature and into tents. Everyone arrived on Saturday morning. A formal flag ceremony was followed by a big troop cheer. Scouts hiked to four campsites nestled in the woods with the peak of Mt Tamalpais off in the distance. Scouts unpacked their camping gear and split into their patrols for advancement activities. There were three advancement stations – knife safety, knots and lashings, and First Aid. Ten new Scouts attended knife safety training, which allows them to carry a pocket knife. Older Scouts worked on knots, lashings and first aid. Each patrol cooked its own meals. After dinner the Troop gathered at the Tamarancho fire ring and amphitheater for a traditional campfire where the patrols put HS ninth grader Romi Bhatia teaches sixth-graders Callum Louch and Thalay Visessonchoke how to interlock their hands and wrists to form a seat to carry an injured person With Trenton Downing on his back, Gabriel Barbosa-Topete practices carrying an injured victim to safety. Upon entering the car, passengers could ask the conductor for a transfer, which allowed them to change to other streetcars for a limited time. Electric streetcars were powered by an overhead electrical wire. A pole on the car contacted the wire and drew power to the traction motors. Each wheel had a traction motor which drove the car. Metal wheels on the metal tracks grounded the cars. Piedmont’s Streetcar Lines Two of the three streetcar lines in Piedmont carried passengers to the small shingled Key Route Station on Piedmont Avenue near 41st Street. There, passengers could stay on the Number 10 car and continue to downtown Oakland. They could also transfer to a streetcar to the ferry terminal on a 16,000-foot pier at the end of Yerba Buena Street in Oakland. There, they would board a ferry to San Francisco. Hugh Craig noted that on a good day it took him 1½ hours to get from his home in Piedmont to his office in San Francisco. Passengers could also transfer to other streetcars at the Piedmont Avenue Station to go to other neighborhoods. At its height, the Key System had over 66 miles of track, and served East Bay residents from Albany to San Leandro. The small Key Route Station was replaced in 1939 by a larger station at 41st and Piedmont Avenues, which became a hub of East Bay transportation for decades. This building still stands, and until recently housed a variety of restaurants. The canopy that protected passengers was demolished in 1961. The Number 10 Streetcar The Number 10 streetcar was the longest line through Piedmont, running from the Piedmont Avenue Station to Crocker Park. It left Piedmont Avenue and turned onto the right-of-way between Grand Avenue and Brandon Street. Today, that right-ofway is a strip of land planted with pine trees. The Number 10 car turned onto the right-of-way on the east side of Arroyo and continued up Ramona and Park Way to Highland Avenue. Today that right-ofway along Arroyo, Ramona and Park Way is filled with mid-century homes. Some history of Highland Ave. Have you ever wondered why Highland Avenue is four lanes wide for a street only five blocks in length? From Park Way, the Number 10 turned south on Highland Avenue where cars and electric streetcars shared the road. The streetcar then turned onto the right-of-way behind stores, now Highland Way. From there, streetcars ran in front of the Community Hall. The parking lot at the Community Hall was built on that right-of-way. From the Community Hall, the streetcar crossed to the east side of Highland and curved onto Sheridan where the large lawn is today. At Caperton, streetcars ran behind homes on Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. Today, you can see mid-century houses at 120 and 129 Caperton, 321 and 322 Sheridan and 463 Wildwood. At the end of the line, the front of the car became the back as the conductor flipped the seat backs from forward to rear facing, and the car reversed its direction back to Piedmont Avenue. The Number 10 line was discontinued in 1948, and the streetcar right-of-ways became home sites and parks. You can follow the Number 10 streetcar route through Piedmont by noting the mid-century houses built in the former right-of-ways. Upon entering the car, passengers could ask the conductor for a transfer, which allowed them to change to other streetcars for a limited time. Electric streetcars were powered by an overhead electrical wire. A pole on the car contacted the wire and drew power to the traction motors. Each wheel had a traction motor which drove the car. Metal wheels on the metal tracks grounded the cars. Piedmont’s Streetcar Lines Two of the three streetcar lines in Piedmont carried passengers to the small shingled Key Route Station on Piedmont Avenue near 41st Street. There, passengers could stay on the Number 10 car and continue to downtown Oakland. They could also transfer to a streetcar to the ferry terminal on a 16,000-foot pier at the end of Yerba Buena Street in Oakland. There, they would board a ferry to San Francisco. Hugh Craig noted that on a good day it took him 1½ hours to get from his home in Piedmont to his office in San Francisco. Passengers could also transfer to other streetcars at the Piedmont Avenue Station to go to other neighborhoods. At its height, the Key System had over 66 miles of track, and served East Bay residents from Albany to San Leandro. The small Key Route Station was replaced in 1939 by a larger station at 41st and Piedmont Avenues, which became a hub of East Bay transportation for decades. This building still stands, and until recently housed a variety of restaurants. The canopy that protected passengers was demolished in 1961. The Number 10 Streetcar The Number 10 streetcar was the longest line through Piedmont, running from the Piedmont Avenue Station to Crocker Park. It left Piedmont Avenue and turned onto the right-of-way between Grand Avenue and Brandon Street. Today, that right-ofway is a strip of land planted with pine trees. The Number 10 car turned onto the right-of-way on the east side of Arroyo and continued up Ramona and Park Way to Highland Avenue. Today that right-ofway along Arroyo, Ramona and Park Way is filled with mid-century homes. Some history of Highland Ave. Have you ever wondered why Highland Avenue is four lanes wide for a street only five blocks in length? From Park Way, the Number 10 turned south on Highland Avenue where cars and electric streetcars shared the road. The streetcar then turned onto the right-of-way behind stores, now Highland Way. From there, streetcars ran in front of the Community Hall. The parking lot at the Community Hall was built on that right-of-way. From the Community Hall, the streetcar crossed to the east side of Highland and curved onto Sheridan where the large lawn is today. At Caperton, streetcars ran behind homes on Sheridan and Wildwood Avenues. Today, you can see mid-century houses at 120 and 129 Caperton, 321 and 322 Sheridan and 463 Wildwood. articles.text: Alameda County announced on Friday, April 23 it would begin administering a COVID-19 vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson again after investigating its connection to a small number of blood clot cases. The county joined other Bay Area counties in following guidance from the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration released that day. The county said it would make more information about the rare blood clotting risks widely available. The CDC recommended that health agencies pause the use of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine on April 13 “out of an abundance of caution” due to reports of severe blood clotting issues in a handful of cases. The Alameda County Public Health Department followed this guidance. As of last week, the CDC has confirmed 17 cases of a blood clotting disorder out of some 8 million people who have received the Johnson & Johnson COVID- 19 vaccine. There have been three reported deaths due to the blood clots. Most of the blood clot cases were in women between the ages of 18 and 48. Symptoms typically occurred 6 to 13 days after vaccination. Due to the exceedingly low rate of blood clots, the CDC found the benefits of the Johnson & Johnson vaccine outweighed the risks and announced that health providers should begin providing it again after a 10-day pause. Alameda County announced it would begin using up its small supply of Johnson & Johnson vaccine as soon as possible. Even though the blood clot disorder appears to be extremely rare, people who receive the Johnson & Johnson vaccine are encouraged to monitor themselves for symptoms, like severe headache, abdominal pain, leg pain or shortness of breath within three weeks after vaccination. Anyone experiencing these symptoms should contact their health care provider immediately. “The public is strongly urged to get vaccinated as soon as possible,” health officers from all Bay Area counties said in a joint statement released Sunday, April 25. “All vaccines are proven to be highly effective at preventing hospitalization or death from COVID-19, and people who are fully vaccinated are also much less likely to be contagious or transmit the virus to someone else. The longer you wait to get vaccinated, the greater the risk of contracting COVID-19, and infecting a friend, loved one or coworker.” Even with the pause on the Johnson & Johnson vaccine, vaccination in Alameda County has continued on a brisk pace. Because the Johnson & Johnson vaccine only requires one shot compared to the two-dose vaccines available from Pfizer and Moderna, health officials hope its reintroduction to the county’s supply will accelerate vaccination even more. In Piedmont, 92 percent of the adult population, about 7,650 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine as of last week. Almost 61 percent of Piedmonters, about 5,000 residents, are now fully vaccinated, the highest percentage in the county. Alameda County has administered over 1.35 million doses of vaccine since December, and over 41 percent of the county’s population is now fully vaccinated. In Oakland, almost 65 percent of the population has received at least one dose and about 41 percent of Oaklanders are fully vaccinated. Overall, the county is hoping to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the population. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents ages 16 and older. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for people ages 18 and older. Pfizer vaccines are currently approved for teenagers as young as 16, and the pharmaceutical company is in the process of seeking authorization for their vaccine for children ages 12 to 15. Less monumental, they are asymmetrical and exhibit many classical motifs including the balustrades (fancy guardrails) and dentils (the small repetitive protrusions at the cornice). The Colonial Revival giveaway is the use of paired columns, not employed in earlier eras, something I think adds an incredible richness to the design. The arches (but not the solar panels) are a Roman contribution. A variant of the Colonial Revival is the Georgian style from England. It is restrained in classical ornamentation but wonderfully proportioned and balanced over the entire symmetrical facade. The Gambrel (double sloped) roof with dormers, and curved eave on this fine home is a characteristic of the Dutch influence, another subcategory of the Colonial Revival genre.
